$comment: Everyday stories, noun Flow, part 1 of 2 (flow, flowHook, flowInput, flowSchedule, awaitMatch, humanTask). Same style rules as stories-pilot.json. Owner reviews each part.

stories.awaitMatch.correlation: A customer's refund waits for the bank's answer, and the bank answers many refunds at once. Correlation, when true, makes the flow resume only for the event that carries the same correlation id as this very flow, so the answer for Ana's refund never wakes Bruno's.
stories.awaitMatch.payload: A flow waits for 'payment received', but only the payment for its own order counts. Payload is a list of tests: each field of the event must equal the value of an expression, such as this order's number. Only then does the event wake the flow.
stories.flow.action: A screen button starts the flow 'Cancel order'. Action says how that button looks: its label, a confirmation question and a danger level, so a risky flow asks 'Are you sure?' before it runs.
stories.flow.concept: A flow that handles orders would repeat 'Order' in every step. Concept names the kind of record the flow works on by default, and every concept step without its own scope uses it.
stories.flow.crossAggregateReason: As a rule, one flow saves changes in one bundle of records, such as one invoice with its lines. A year-end flow that must touch invoices and stock together is an exception. This keyword is the written reason that allows it, and it is mandatory, for that flow only.
stories.flow.description: Six months from now, a new colleague opens the flow 'Close month' and wonders what it is for. Description is one or two sentences that answer, for people and for AI helpers who write models.
stories.flow.hooks: A pack supplies a ready-made flow for orders, and a shop only wants to add a step: 'warn the warehouse' right after 'confirm payment'. Hooks are those added steps, each placed before or after a named step of the base flow.
stories.flow.input: A flow 'Register customer' should ask for exactly what the customer concept holds, without listing every box again. Input says the flow's input has the same shape as a request body of that concept.
stories.flow.inputSchema: A flow that sends an invoice needs an invoice number and an e-mail. Input schema describes what the flow must be given, so a call with something missing or of the wrong kind is refused at the door.
stories.flow.metadata: Sometimes a flow cannot be written as steps, and a developer supplies a Java class of their own. Metadata binds that class to the flow, pinned by its hash, so it runs instead of the steps. It is a way out for rare needs.
stories.flow.name: Buttons, other flows and AI helpers need a name to call a flow by, such as 'ShipOrder'. Name is that handle, unique in the model. It becomes part of the flow's address in the API.
stories.flow.outputSchema: A flow 'Quote price' returns a number and a currency. Output schema describes the value of its return step, so whoever calls the flow knows exactly what comes back.
stories.flow.specializes: A pack offers a standard 'Order approval' flow, and a shop wants it almost as it is. Specializes names that base flow, and the new one only adds hooks instead of copying all the steps.
stories.flow.startEndpoint: Some flows are started by a person or a system through an address of the generated app. Start endpoint says whether such an address is offered for this flow. Expose is the current, finer way to say who may start it.
stories.flow.steps: A flow is a recipe: check the stock, reserve it, send the e-mail. Steps are the ordered list of those actions. At least one is needed, unless the flow specializes another and only adds hooks.
stories.flowHook.position: A shop wants to warn the warehouse just after payment is confirmed. Position says whether the hook's steps run before or after the step they attach to.
stories.flowHook.steps: The warning to the warehouse is itself one or two small steps. Steps are those inserted steps, and at least one is needed.
stories.flowHook.targetStep: To add a step after 'confirm payment', NPDev has to know which step that is. Target step names the step of the base flow the hook attaches to.
stories.flowInput.concept: A flow that creates customers should accept what the customer form accepts. Concept names the kind of record whose request body the flow's input copies.
stories.flowInput.mode: The same concept has different bodies for creating, changing, deleting and querying. Mode picks which one the flow's input mirrors: create, update, delete or query.
stories.flowSchedule.cron: A bakery wants the flow 'Send tomorrow's orders' to run every day at five in the morning. Cron is that timetable, written in the classic five fields, minute, hour, day, month and weekday, or in six with seconds.
stories.flowSchedule.tenantScope: A software company serves many customer accounts, and each should get its own nightly run. Tenant scope lists the accounts the flow runs for, with one independent schedule each. If you say nothing, only the default account is used.
stories.humanTask.assignee: A purchase above a limit must be approved by a person, not by the system. Assignee says who may complete the task: a specific user, one or more roles, or both.
stories.humanTask.description: The task title says 'Approve purchase', but the approver needs details. Description is a longer text shown with the task in the inbox.
stories.humanTask.fields: To approve a refund, the manager must also write a reason and the amount agreed. Fields are the little form the person fills in, and what they type travels with the completed event.
stories.humanTask.outcomeField: The manager's choice, approve or reject, has to be saved somewhere the flow can read it. Outcome field names the key that receives the chosen outcome. If you say nothing, it is called outcome.
stories.humanTask.outcomes: The approver sees two buttons, 'Approve' and 'Reject'. Outcomes are those buttons, at least one, each with a value and a label. The chosen value is stored under the outcome field.
stories.humanTask.proposal: An AI helper proposes changes to a customer's record, and a person must review them. Proposal turns the task into a review: the inbox shows the proposed values beside the current ones, field by field, and the completed event carries what was accepted.
stories.humanTask.record: The task 'Check this order' should lead the approver straight to that order. Record points to the business record the task is about, which must carry an id, and the inbox links to it.
stories.humanTask.title: The inbox of an approver lists many tasks, so each one needs a clear heading such as 'Approve purchase PO-1042'. Title is that heading, and placeholders such as the saved record's code are filled in from the flow's data.
